note: Official strategies, consultations, committee reports, process orders and draft instruments that shape Indian AI governance but are not binding law. Each quote is an exact excerpt from the named source, with line breaks normalized. Status is shown separately from the binding-law corpus.

documents.title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence
documents.sourceTitle: NITI Aayog, National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (June 2018)
documents.quote: #AIforAll means technology leadership in AI for achieving the greater good.
documents.relevance: The origin of the AI for All frame: growth and inclusion, with privacy, security and intellectual property named as cross-cutting concerns.

documents.title: Responsible AI for All: Principles for Responsible AI (Part 1)
documents.sourceTitle: NITI Aayog, Responsible AI for All: Principles for Responsible AI (February 2021)
documents.quote: the principles for responsible AI are derived from the Constitution of India and various laws enacted thereunder.
documents.relevance: Grounds the seven principles in constitutional rights, not in a standalone AI code. It remains a discussion paper.

documents.title: Responsible AI for All: Operationalizing Principles for Responsible AI (Part 2)
documents.sourceTitle: NITI Aayog, Operationalizing Principles for Responsible AI (August 2021)
documents.quote: Ensuring that AI systems adhere to the principles requires a multi-disciplinary approach and a behavioral shift in organizational processes and practices.
documents.relevance: Moves from principles to procurement, process and institutional practice. It is guidance, not a compliance instrument.

documents.title: Responsible AI for All: Adopting the Framework — A Use Case Approach on Facial Recognition Technology
documents.sourceTitle: NITI Aayog, Responsible AI for All: Adopting the Framework — Facial Recognition Technology (November 2022)
documents.quote: This draft discussion paper is being released for seeking public comments.
documents.relevance: Tests the responsible-AI framework on facial recognition, the biometric use case closest to identity, surveillance and privacy harms.

documents.title: AI for Viksit Bharat: The Opportunity for Accelerated Economic Growth
documents.sourceTitle: NITI Aayog, AI for Viksit Bharat (September 2025)
documents.quote: robust AI governance frameworks, including ethics guidelines and risk controls, could ensure responsible and secure deployment.
documents.relevance: The current NITI AI document shifts emphasis from ethics to growth and adoption, while still naming governance and risk controls.

documents.title: AI for Inclusive Societal Development: A Roadmap for India's Informal Workforce
documents.sourceTitle: NITI Aayog, AI for Inclusive Societal Development (October 2025)
documents.quote: the true measure of technological progress is not simply in productivity gains or economic growth, but in its power to transform lives with dignity, opportunity, and hope.
documents.relevance: Places India's 490 million informal workers at the centre of AI adoption. Labour is otherwise thin in Indian AI policy.

documents.title: India AI Governance Guidelines
documents.quote: India has developed a pragmatic approach to AI governance that is emphasised by a techno-legal framework supported by voluntary measures and Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI).
documents.relevance: The current national framework is voluntary and techno-legal. It explicitly does not create a standalone AI Act or a new AI regulator.

documents.title: Working Paper on Generative AI and Copyright, Part I: One Nation One License One Payment
documents.issuer: DPIIT Committee on Generative AI and Copyright
documents.sourceTitle: DPIIT, Working Paper on Generative AI and Copyright, Part I (December 2025)
documents.quote: The first part examines the legal and regulatory issues pertaining to the large-scale unlicensed use of copyrighted materials for training of generative artificial intelligence tools
documents.quoteNote: Part II, on authorship, moral rights and output liability, had not been published at retrieval.
documents.relevance: The central copyright consultation. A majority recommended a mandatory blanket licence with statutory remuneration, not a broad text-and-data-mining exception. No amendment is in force.

documents.title: Impact of Emergence of Artificial Intelligence and Related Issues — Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology (27th Report)
documents.sourceTitle: PRS Legislative Research, summary of the 27th Report of the Standing Committee on Communications and IT (1 April 2026)
documents.quote: The Committee recommended: (i) expediting implementation of draft amendments to the IT Rules, (ii) exploring possibility of a comprehensive legislation to prevent misuse of AI, and (iii) exploring age restrictions for certain platforms
documents.relevance: A cross-party recommendation for a comprehensive AI-misuse statute and platform age limits. It is a recommendation, not law; the source here is the published summary.

documents.title: Draft Regulations for Use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, 2026
documents.issuer: Artificial Intelligence Committee, Supreme Court of India
documents.sourceTitle: Supreme Court AI Committee, draft regulations and notice (3 June 2026; comments extended to 15 July 2026)
documents.quote: These regulations aim to govern the use of Artificial Intelligence in Courts, grounded in the principles of human primacy, transparency, accountability, data protection, and judicial independence
documents.relevance: The judiciary's own draft guardrails for AI use in courts. They are not notified and do not bind litigants or the public.

documents.title: Draft Guidelines on Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence in Telecommunication Networks and Provision of Telecommunication Services
documents.sourceTitle: TRAI, draft AI guidelines for telecom (30 October 2026; comments close 27 November 2026)
documents.quote: All AI systems shall be subject to an appropriate human oversight for risk mitigation as per a predefined mechanism.
documents.relevance: A board-approved AI policy, risk tiers, an AI-system inventory, incident reporting and human oversight for telecom licensees. It is still a consultation draft.

documents.title: FREE-AI Committee Report: Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of Artificial Intelligence
documents.quote: Entities that deploy AI should be responsible and remain fully accountable for the decisions and outcomes that arise from the use of these systems, regardless of their level of automation or autonomous functioning. Accountability should be clearly assigned. Accountability cannot be delegated to the model and underlying algorithm.
documents.relevance: The committee recommends entity accountability, board oversight and sectoral governance; it is not a direction and creates no compliance duty. RBI’s binding technology-neutral directions still do the operative work.

documents.title: Office Order: Working Group on Artificial Intelligence (AI) Governance in the Insurance Sector
documents.issuer: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India
documents.type: Office order constituting a working group
documents.sourceTitle: IRDAI, Office Order No. IRDAI/GA&HR/ORD/MISC/90/06/2026 (17 June 2026)
documents.quote: In order to ensure that the industry is adequately prepared to harness these technologies responsibly and safeguarding the interests of policyholders, it is essential to study their impact on insurance ecosystem as they also introduce new dimensions of ethical, operational, and cyber security risks.
documents.relevance: Constitutes a seven-member working group and sets its terms of reference, including a proposed AI governance framework and pre- and post-deployment audit. It is not an AI rule, and no report had been published at retrieval.
